## Result: not 3-colorable

I found a subgraph that cannot be 3-colored, so the whole graph cannot be either.

**Forcing argument.** Use colors {0,1,2} and consider the nodes {5, 13, 24, 16, 23, 21, 28, 22, 25}.

1. Nodes 5, 13, 24 form a triangle (edges 5-13, 5-24, 13-24), so they receive three distinct colors. Call them c(5), c(13), c(24).
2. Node 16 is adjacent to 5 and 24, so c(16) must be the third color, which is c(13).
3. Node 23 is adjacent to 5 and 16, so c(23) must be the remaining color, which is c(24).
4. Node 21 is adjacent to 13 and 23, so c(21) = c(5).
5. Node 28 is adjacent to 21 and 23, so c(28) = c(13).
6. Node 22 is adjacent to 23 and 28, so c(22) = c(5).
7. Node 25 is adjacent to 13, 23, and 22. Its neighbors use c(13), c(24), and c(5), which are all three colors, so 25 has no valid color.

Every edge used in this chain appears in the given edge list (e.g., [5,16], [16,23], [21,23], [21,28], [22,28], [22,25], [23,25], [13,25]). Since the choice of colors for 5, 13, 24 was arbitrary, the contradiction holds for every 3-coloring attempt, and no spilling is allowed.
